name: StringZilla (StringWars shootout evidence)
language: C (kernels) with C++, Rust and Python bindings
baseline: Rust std str::find and rfind, the memchr crate (memmem::find, Finder, rfind, FinderRev), Python str.find and rfind, and regex, bstr and aho_corasick for byte sets; the StringWars harness has no libc strstr or std::string rows
workload: StringWars find benchmarks: forward and reverse exact substring search over short-word queries and long lines, and byte-set search, on a text corpus with warm-up, run with RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=native'.
claimed_speedup: Intel Xeon4 Sapphire Rapids, 'Measured June 17, 2026' (find/README.md): forward search short words stringzilla::find 11.41 GB/s vs std::str::find 9.34, memmem::find 9.52, memmem::Finder 9.99; long lines 11.52 vs 11.45, 11.29, 11.33 (parity). Reverse search short words stringzilla::rfind 10.79 vs std::str::rfind 2.94, memmem::rfind 2.93, memmem::FinderRev 2.96 (3.7x derived from page data); long lines 11.45 vs 5.21, 5.02, 5.02. Byte-set search long lines stringzilla find_byteset 8.34 vs regex::find_iter 5.07, aho_corasick 0.51 GB/s. Python: stringzilla Str.find 3.37 vs str.find 0.73 GB/s (short), 11.64 vs 1.14 (long). The top-level README chart shows memmem::Finder 10.99 ahead of stringzilla 10.82 GB/s for forward long-line search.
compiler_and_flags: RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=native' cargo bench (find/bench.rs); Rust toolchain version not stated in the files opened
hardware: Intel Xeon4 Sapphire Rapids (SKU not stated); other tables in the README use Granite Rapids and H100/RTX 6000 Pro GPUs
tradeoffs: StringZilla is the library; StringWars is the benchmark repo. AVX2/AVX-512, NEON, SVE and SWAR backends with runtime dispatch; the C API is callable from C++. The license above is StringZilla's (Apache 2.0 or three-clause BSD per its README); the StringWars repo has no LICENSE file at its root.
caveats: The shootout is run by StringZilla's author, and its baselines are Rust and Python incumbents, not glibc or std::string. For the libc and C++ baselines only the first-party StringZilla README exists: on Xeon4 with glibc, libc strstr 21.3 GB/s vs sz_find 21.0 GB/s (a tie), std::string::find 9.1 GB/s (2.3x derived), while on the Apple M5 Pro libc strstr is 3.5 vs 37.1 GB/s; the README itself says the libc gap is largely a library difference. Forward long-line search is at parity with std::str::find and memchr's memmem.

tradeoffs: Interpreter: steady-state execution is about 10x behind optimising JITs, so the win is over other interpreters and in startup (lazy compilation), not over Wasmtime Cranelift or V8 peak speed. Lazy modes defer compile and validation cost to first call ('lazy.unchecked' also skips validation, which is only safe for trusted modules). Pure safe-ish Rust, no_std friendly, runs where JITs cannot (iOS, embedded, wasm itself).
caveats: Suite and plots are run by the Wasmi maintainers (first-party for Wasmi, but code, flags and CPU models are public so tier A applies). Plot values are 'relative time vs. optimal runtime' (geometric mean over test cases of the ratio to the fastest runtime on each case, lower is better), read from the SVG text of the geomean plots, not from a table; run dates are not stated on the plots (suite commits date from Aug-Sep 2026). Wasmi v2 in the suite is v2.0.0-beta.7; Wasmi 2.0.0 was prepared for release on 2026-09-01 (commit 'Prepare Wasmi v2.0.0 release'). baseline: Wasmtime (Cranelift)
workload: libsodium's built-in benchmark suite (61 crypto and utility tests) compiled once to WebAssembly and run on iwasm, Wasmtime, Wasmer (Cranelift, LLVM, Singlepass), WasmEdge, wazero, wasm2c, Node, Bun and wasm3, with native code as reference.

Against native its geometric-mean time is 2.30x, versus 3.46x for Wasmtime, 3.35x for WasmEdge and 3.91x for Node (derived from page data).
tradeoffs: The iwasm CSV does not say whether it ran the AOT compiler output (wamrc) or an interpreter; an interpreter cannot plausibly reach these times, so AOT is assumed. AOT needs a separate compile step and LLVM at build time; the fast interpreter and JIT modes trade this differently.

claimed_speedup: Execute geomean (lower is better), V8 vs Wasmtime Cranelift / Wasmer Cranelift: EPYC 7763 1.05 vs 1.15 / 1.17; i7700 1.13 vs 1.25 / 1.24; Xeon 8573C 1.04 vs 1.21 / 1.21; on Apple M2 Pro 1.22 vs 1.27 / 1.28 and M4 Pro 1.19 vs 1.31 / 1.31 (Silverfir-nano's JIT is first there at 1.06 and 1.07). Startup geomean: EPYC 7763 V8 33.27 vs Wasmtime Cranelift 1634.19, Wasmer Cranelift 1484.15, Wasmtime Winch 298.15, Wasmer Singlepass 162.12 (about 49x faster than Wasmtime Cranelift, derived from page data); M4 Pro 21.11 vs 1198.20, 1155.05, 185.66, 101.26.

Runtime pins read from runtimes/*/Cargo.toml: wasmtime 47.0.0, wasmer 7.2.0, v8 crate 150.1.0, wasmi 2.0.0-beta.10 (README links v2.0.0-beta.7), Silverfir-nano git tag 0.5, wasm3 via wasm3x 0.2.1 (Wasm3 v0.9.0), WAMR fast interpreter via wamrx 0.3, stitch from Robbepop/stitch branch v0.1-dev. rustc version not stated (no rust-toolchain file).
hardware: AMD EPYC 7763, Apple M2 Pro, Apple M4 Pro, Intel i7700 (as titled in the plots), Intel Xeon Platinum 8573C (CPU names read from the plot titles and data directories of wasmi-benchmarks-plots; core counts, RAM and OS not stated)
stars_or_usage: 25.3k stars (GitHub mirror); engine of Chrome and Node.js
tradeoffs: Large C++ dependency embedded through a prebuilt Rust crate in this harness; tiered compilation (lazy Liftoff baseline, then TurboFan) trades peak throughput for startup.
caveats: Evidence for an already catalogued project. The geomean plots report each runtime's time relative to a theoretical optimal runtime (the fastest runtime on every test), so lower is better and 1.00 is optimal; values were read from the rendered SVG plots in wasmi-benchmarks-plots (plots updated 2025-08-25 to 2026-08-27) and CoreMark scores from data/<machine>/coremark.json in wasmi-benchmarks (higher is better; no Xeon 8573C coremark.json, and the Apple M2 Pro file has no JIT rows). The suite is maintained by the Wasmi maintainer (Robbepop), so it is not neutral for Wasmi and the forked Stitch branch. Only the geomean plots were read, not the per-test plots or raw criterion.json. Test inputs are mostly Rust programs compiled to Wasm. V8 is not uniformly ahead: on CoreMark the Cranelift engines score higher (EPYC 7763 20822 vs Wasmtime 23011 and Wasmer 22199; M4 Pro 35334 vs 38969 and 38434; i7700 19470 vs 23231 and 23454). V8's startup advantage over the Rust JITs reflects lazy tiered compilation, and Wasmi's lazy modes start about 20 to 30x faster still.
